claims.text: The baseline near-equiatomic lightweight high-entropy alloy typically forms a multiphase microstructure.
A homogeneous single-phase solid solution is the key mechanism enabling low density, high strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance simultaneously.
Uniform atomic distribution in a single-phase solid solution creates controlled lattice distortion.
Changing the ratios of low-density or oxygen-affine elements can force formation of a homogeneous single-phase solid solution instead of a multiphase structure.
Lattice distortion in the single-phase structure hinders dislocation motion.
Dislocation pinning caused by uniform lattice distortion increases mechanical strength.
A uniform single-phase lattice favors formation of a coherent, stable, and adherent protective surface oxide.
The protective oxide improves corrosion resistance.
The protective oxide improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Formation of the single-phase structure preserves low overall alloy density.
A multiphase microstructure produces localized stress concentrations.
A multiphase microstructure produces inhomogeneous oxide growth.
Secondary or intermetallic phases compromise the targeted combination of properties.
The single-phase alloy will have greater mechanical strength than the baseline multiphase alloy.
The single-phase alloy will have greater corrosion resistance than the baseline multiphase alloy.
The single-phase alloy will have greater high-temperature oxidation resistance than the baseline multiphase alloy.
The single-phase alloy will retain low density relative to the intended lightweight baseline.
Changing composition beyond solubility limits will produce significant fractions of secondary brittle intermetallic phases.
Service temperatures beyond the protective oxide's stability range will destabilize the oxide layer.
Loss of protective-oxide stability will eliminate the proposed performance benefits of the single-phase structure.

contradictions.description: The conditions require identical processing for the control and modified alloys, while the experimental design refers to a modified composition/process. If processing itself is modified, the comparison is not processed identically and phase structure is confounded with processing.
